title: A Letter for the Typewriter
premise: In the autumn of 1913, Juniper Fairweather serves as driver and courier for the formidable suffragist Adeline Marsh, secretly reading every letter that passes through their hands and memorizing other people's lives to fill the silence of their own. When the seasonal bridge closes, trapping the household with a dying matriarch, a fugitive printer, and Adeline's estranged daughter, Juniper's careful invisibility collapses as old letters surface revealing Juniper's own buried connection to the family. As a ship prepares to sail on the morning tide with only one berth secured by Adeline, Juniper must decide whether loyalty means protecting the woman they serve or telling the truth that will shatter the found family they've built. In the end, Juniper gives the berth away, stays behind, and chooses truth — discovering that the family worth having is the one that survives being seen.
about_author: Mirabel Blackwood is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unsent letters in provincial record offices, where she first encountered the quiet revolutionaries history forgot to file. She writes from a converted coach house, where a 1910 typewriter sits on her desk as both tool and muse.

chapters.title: The Weight of Paper
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Establishing the rhythms of service: driving Adeline Marsh between suffrage meetings, memorizing letters Juniper has no right to read but cannot stop reading. A letter arrives that makes Juniper's hands shake — addressed to Adeline in handwriting Juniper recognizes from childhood. Beat: the comfort of invisibility, and its first crack.

chapters.title: What the River Decides
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. The county announces the bridge will close for repairs until spring, severing the town. Adeline decides to stay at the estate with her ailing mother, Cordelia, and summons her estranged daughter, Vivian. Juniper watches the household assemble like pieces of a machine built to explode. Beat: dread disguised as duty.

chapters.title: Vivian at the Gate
chapters.summary: Alternating Juniper and Vivian POVs. Vivian arrives hostile and sharp-tongued, seeing Juniper as furniture. But a shared cigarette on the back steps cracks the surface — Vivian recognizes something in Juniper's face, though she can't name it. Beat: the dangerous beginning of being perceived.

chapters.title: Cordelia's Drawer
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Summoned to Cordelia's room to sort correspondence, Juniper finds letters from twenty years ago — including one written by Juniper's own mother, a housemaid dismissed in disgrace. Cordelia, lucid in a rare moment, tells Juniper: 'I know whose eyes you have.' Beat: the past stops being abstract.

chapters.title: The Printer in the Cellar
chapters.summary: Vivian's POV. Vivian discovers a fugitive printer, Elias, hiding in the wine cellar — a suffrage pressman wanted for sedition, smuggled in by Adeline. Instead of exposing him, she begins helping him, finding purpose she never had in London. Beat: loyalty to a cause versus loyalty to a family, the novel's engine ignites.

chapters.title: Letters Never Sent
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper confronts Adeline with the old letter, demanding to know why her mother was dismissed. Adeline's answer is half-truth, and Juniper recognizes the evasions because Juniper has spent a lifetime crafting them. First real rupture between servant and mistress. Beat: anger as a form of hope.

chapters.title: The Berth
chapters.summary: Adeline's POV. News arrives that a ship sails on the morning tide with passage secured for one — arranged to spirit Elias out of the country. Adeline must choose who takes it, weighing her daughter, the fugitive, and the driver who has become something she refuses to name. Beat: the weight of command, and its loneliness.

chapters.title: What Vivian Saw
chapters.summary: Vivian's POV. Vivian finds Juniper's hidden collection of copied letters and realizes Juniper has been reading everything — including Vivian's own most private correspondence to a woman in Paris. Betrayed, she threatens to expose Juniper and Elias both. Beat: the climax of secrets; every alliance inverts.

chapters.title: The Morning Tide
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. The night before departure, Cordelia dies peacefully, having extracted a deathbed promise from Adeline: the truth, told whole. At dawn, Juniper publicly gives the berth to Elias, confesses everything — the letters, the mother, the reading — before the whole household. Beat: the climax; truth as sacrifice.

chapters.title: A Letter for the Typewriter
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV, months later. The bridge reopens; Adeline, changed, offers Juniper not a job but a partnership, and Vivian stays through winter. Juniper sits at Cordelia's old typewriter and writes the first letter meant to be read by its recipient — addressed to the mother who may still be alive. Beat: resolution; memory transformed from burden into inheritance.
